content: Turning 100 is unusually common in one Sardinian village, and centuries of records help show that its residents’ remarkable ages are real. Women in Bolotana, a mountain community of about 2,300 people on the Italian island of Sardinia, have an exceptional pattern of survival after age 70. An international study suggests the village could qualify as a new “blue zone,” a community known for unusually long lives, although more observation is needed to establish that status. Researchers estimated that women who reach 70 have a 13.8% chance of living to 100, compared with approximately 3.5% in Italy and 3.6% in the United States. That puts Bolotana’s estimate at nearly four times the U.S. figure. The National Geographic-supported study was published in Frontiers in Aging and co-authored by S. Jay Olshansky, professor emeritus of epidemiology at the University of Illinois Chicago School of Public Health. Bolotana first drew attention because six residents were at least 100 years old in 2024. Relative to the village’s population, the researchers estimated that centenarians were roughly 11 times as common as in the United States. But a high count alone cannot establish exceptional longevity, making reliable age records essential. “What makes Bolotana extraordinary is that it has an incredible historical record that allows us to definitively evaluate ages at birth and death,” Olshansky said. “The municipal and baptismal records date back centuries and allowed us to independently verify ages.” The team reconstructed residents’ life histories across more than a century, matching birth, baptismal and death records. Among 3,060 people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925, researchers documented 38 who reached 100. “Every single person that has made it past 100, we can validate,” Olshansky said. “There is no ambiguity.” Sardinia’s original blue zone, identified more than two decades ago, became famous for exceptional male longevity. Bolotana presents a different pattern: women showed the strongest survival advantage, with nearly 21 years of estimated remaining life expectancy at age 70. The researchers examined both remaining life expectancy at 70 and the likelihood of reaching 100. Among the international benchmarks included, Bolotana’s women ranked second only to Hong Kong on both measures. “Females almost always live longer than males anywhere in the world, but in Sardinia that wasn’t the case. It’s one of the things that made it so unusual,” Olshansky said. “We think this is the longest-lived female population in the world, or close to it.” Blue zones, including Okinawa in Japan and Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula, offer opportunities to investigate why some communities outlive surrounding populations. Bolotana may provide another setting, particularly for studying women’s survival in later life. The village’s archives address a recurring criticism of longevity research: that extraordinary ages sometimes reflect inaccurate documentation. Researchers could check Bolotana’s centenarians against multiple independent sources rather than relying on a single record. However, verified ages do not settle whether the village has a lasting survival advantage. Bolotana’s estimates varied with the calendar period analyzed, and earlier years showed a less pronounced advantage, particularly for survival to 100. Longer observation and continued demographic validation are needed before researchers can consider it an established blue zone. The study also did not determine what causes the longevity pattern. Walking, food, family relationships, and genetics are possible contributors, but the demographic findings cannot establish how much each factor matters. Bolotana’s steep streets and hills make physical activity part of ordinary routines. Much of the food is grown locally, including olives used to produce oil rich in healthy fats. Families often live near one another, and social isolation appears uncommon. “You’ve got this close-knit community where people take care of each other,” Olshansky said. “Movement is largely done by walking, not by driving.” These features give researchers several connected possibilities to investigate. Daily movement, diet, and social support may work alongside inherited traits, making the village’s longevity difficult to trace to any single habit. “If we can identify the characteristics behind this longevity and help people adopt them, the rest of the world can benefit from understanding the values practiced by these communities.” Reference: “A new blue zone? exceptional late-life survival in Bolotana, Sardinia” by Giovanni Mario Pes, Steven N. Austad, Dan Buettner, Salvatore Pedde, Vittorio Romerio, Hiram Beltrán-Sánchez and S. Jay Olshansky, 8 September 2026, Frontiers in Aging . Researchers discovered that a diabetes medication altered how certain immune cells function, potentially reducing harmful inflammation. A medication already used to treat diabetes may protect the heart by changing how immune cells behave in the bloodstream. In a small human clinical trial, researchers found that the drug reduced inflammatory cell clusters associated with cardiovascular disease, with measurable effects appearing after just two weeks. The findings, published in the American Heart Association journal Circulation , provide the first direct evidence that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors can alter specific immune cells in humans. These medications are known for lowering blood sugar, promoting weight loss, and providing cardiovascular and kidney benefits, but their effects on inflammation have been less clear. Researchers at Vanderbilt Health studied 16 women with obesity and prediabetes who received the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin for three months. Blood samples collected before treatment, after two weeks, and after 12 weeks allowed investigators to track changes in immune activity. The team also examined a separate comparison group of women who followed a low-calorie diet for three months. Using advanced genetic sequencing and cellular imaging, the researchers identified a significant reduction in monocyte platelet aggregates (MPAs). These clusters form when blood-clotting cells (platelets) attach to immune cells (monocytes), creating structures associated with inflammation in blood vessels and cardiovascular disease. MPA levels declined significantly within two weeks of starting empagliflozin and fell further by the end of the study. The women in the diet comparison group did not show the same reduction, suggesting that the medication’s effects on these cells may extend beyond its influence on body weight. The researchers also identified evidence of “metabolic reprogramming” in monocytes (immune cells). These cells shifted away from a highly inflammatory state toward a more stable metabolic profile associated with normal cellular energy production. “There had been some suggestive studies in animals with these medications indicating they might be modulating the immune system — affecting inflammation — but that hadn’t really been shown in humans,” said Mona Mashayekhi, MD, PhD, Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Division of Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism at Vanderbilt Health. “This study provides the first direct evidence of SGLT2 inhibitors altering human immune cells, which may potentially reduce cardiovascular risk.” “This finding is significant because it’s the first time this medication has been shown to have an immune effect at the cellular level with some specificity. If we understand how these medicines are reducing obesity-associated inflammation and heart disease and kidney disease, then we can identify the best patient for this treatment or discover other drug targets in that pathway that could really be beneficial.” Mashayekhi and her colleagues have launched a randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Vanderbilt Health that aims to enroll 74 participants with obesity and metabolic syndrome. The study will examine immune changes over three months and analyze adipose tissue (fat) to investigate how the medication affects inflammation within the body. The larger trial will help determine whether the immune changes observed in the initial study can be confirmed under more rigorous conditions and clarify how SGLT2 inhibitors influence inflammation associated with metabolic disease. Reference: “SGLT2 Inhibitor Empagliflozin Reduces Circulating Monocyte-Platelet Aggregates: A Pilot Study” by B. Ilkin Safa, Jared M. Oakes, Joshua D. Simmons, Hui Nian, Leslie A. Kirk, Anna C. A hormone that raises blood sugar may help put the brakes on a post-meal spike when fat reaches the gut before sugar. An international research team found that giving mice fat before glucose slowed stomach emptying and reduced the early blood sugar spike. The experiments suggest that the response involves cooperation between gut and pancreatic hormones and nerve signals, offering clues to why food order may matter. Human studies have already shown that eating vegetables, protein, or fat before carbohydrates can moderate post-meal blood sugar rises, an important treatment target in diabetes. Meal sequencing could therefore offer a practical dietary strategy that changes eating order without eliminating foods. “Our group has long been interested in practical dietary approaches that people can continue in everyday life,” says corresponding author Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University. “Meal sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups.” The stomach helps control how quickly nutrients reach the intestine. Slower emptying can spread out glucose delivery, tempering the early blood sugar rise. Researchers have also linked meal-sequencing benefits to increased release of incretin hormones, including GLP-1, which help lower blood glucose. Less clear was how these hormones interact with pancreatic hormones and nerve pathways. To investigate, the team fasted mice overnight and compared three feeding sequences: water followed by glucose, olive oil followed by glucose 15 minutes later, and glucose followed by olive oil 15 minutes later. They tracked blood glucose and plasma levels of insulin, glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. Blood measurements after oral acetaminophen provided an estimate of stomach-emptying speed. When olive oil came first, the mice showed a smaller early blood sugar rise and slower stomach emptying than when it came afterward. Giving fat first also increased early secretion of glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. These effects persisted in mice with type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency. Glucagon is best known for raising blood glucose, making its contribution here particularly intriguing. Blocking either glucagon or GLP-1 signaling alone did not weaken the glucose-lowering effect of giving olive oil first, but blocking both did, indicating that both pathways contribute to the response. The researchers also tested mice lacking the GLP-1 receptor and examined nerve involvement by tying off the vagus nerve below the diaphragm on both sides. The nerve experiments suggested that vagal pathways contribute to the response. Tests with other dietary fats helped establish that the findings were not unique to olive oil. “Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine,” says Yabe. Together with existing clinical evidence, the findings strengthen the case for testing practical meal-sequencing strategies in people with and without diabetes. The next challenge is to determine how reliably this hormone and nerve response translates into benefits during everyday meals. Reference: “Olive Oil Before Oral Glucose Delays Gastric Emptying and Lowers Glycemia Through Partially Redundant Glucagon and GLP-1 Signaling in Mice” by Yanyan Liu, Hiromi Tsuchida, Sodai Kubota, Saki Kubota-Okamoto, Takehiro Kato, Yukio Horikawa, Shin Tsunekawa, Hitoshi Kuwata, Yuuka Fujiwara, Yuji Yamazaki, Yuichiro Yamada, Hiroki Fujita, Katsumi Iizuka, Naoya Murao, Shinji Ueno, Yusuke Seino, Atsushi Suzuki, Yoshitaka Hayashi, Tsuyoshi Nakanishi, Daniel J.
